label: thm:informal
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Informal

label: prop:bijection
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:bijection}
The maps
\[
 c(X)\longmapsto p(X)
 \quad\text{where}\quad
 \frac{X^{2^h}-X}{c(X)}=p(X)^2+X,
\qquad
 p(X)\longmapsto
 c(X)=\frac{X^{2^h}-X}{p(X)^2+X}
\]
are mutually inverse bijections between $\mathcal B_K(D)$ and
$\mathcal L_K(D)$. In fact, every polynomial in $\mathcal L_K(D)$ has
degree exactly $D/2$ and agreement exactly $D$. Consequently,
\[
 A(2^h,D)=|\mathcal L_K(D)|.
\]
head: environment
name: Weight-$D$ BCH words are an exact RS list

title: Proof
body_md:
Take $c\in\mathcal B_K(D)$. It vanishes at exactly $2^h-D$ elements of $K$, so the degree bound is tight: $\deg c=2^h-D$. Hence $c$ splits into distinct linear factors over $K$, all among the factors of
\[
 X^{2^h}-X=\prod_{\beta\in K}(X-\beta),
\]
and therefore $c\mid X^{2^h}-X$. Write
\[
 b(X)=\frac{X^{2^h}-X}{c(X)}.
\]
Then $\deg b=D$, and its roots are exactly the $D$ points where $c(\beta)=1$.

Differentiating
\[
 b(X)c(X)=X^{2^h}-X
\]
gives, in characteristic two,
\[
 b'(X)c(X)+b(X)c'(X)=1.
\]
At every root $\beta$ of $b$ we have $c(\beta)=1$, hence $b'(\beta)=1$. Since $b'(X)-1$ has degree at most $D-1$ and at least $D$ roots, $b'(X)=1$ identically.

Write $b(X)=\sum_j b_jX^j$. In characteristic two, differentiation kills the even powers, so $b'(X)=1$ says that the only odd-degree term of $b$ is $X$. Thus $b(X)-X$ contains only even powers. Because squaring is an automorphism of the finite field $K$, its coefficients have unique square roots, and there is a unique $p\in K[X]$ such that
\[
 b(X)=p(X)^2+X.
\]
Since $D$ is even, $\deg p=D/2$. At every root $\beta$ of $b$ we have $p(\beta)^2=\beta$, hence $p(\beta)=\beta^{2^{h-1}}$. Thus $p\in\mathcal L_K(D)$.

Conversely, let $p\in\mathcal L_K(D)$ and set $b=p^2+X$. Then $b'=1$, while $\deg b\le D$ and the agreement condition gives at least $D$ distinct roots in $K$. Hence $\deg b=D$ and these are exactly its roots. Therefore $b\mid X^{2^h}-X$, and
\[
 c(X)=\frac{X^{2^h}-X}{b(X)}
\]
has degree $2^h-D$. At a nonroot of $b$ we have $c(\beta)=0$; at a root, the differentiated identity above gives $c(\beta)=1$ because $b'(\beta)=1$. Hence $c\in\mathcal B_K(D)$. The two constructions are inverse by definition.
head: environment

label: rem:binary-obstruction
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:binary-obstruction}
Since $c$ is $\mathbb F_2$-valued, it equals one
at every root of the complementary factor $b$.
Differentiating $bc=X^{2^h}-X$ therefore gives
$b'(\beta)=1$ at all its $D$ roots, and the
degree bound implies $b'\equiv1$. Over odd
characteristic, nonzero BCH symbols need not agree,
so the analogous derivative values
$-c(\beta)^{-1}$ need not be constant.
This is the obstruction to this particular
BCH--RS correspondence in odd characteristic.
head: environment
name: Where characteristic two enters

label: prop:additive
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:additive}
Let $V\le K$ be an additive subspace and put
$n_0:=|V|$ and $\nu_V:=\ell_V'\in K^*$. For even $2\le D<n_0$, there is a bijection
between
\[
 \left\{g\in K[X]:
   \deg g\le n_0-D,\ g(V)\subseteq\mathbb F_2,\ \operatorname{wt}_V(g)=D
 \right\}
\]
and the polynomials $p\in K[X]$ of degree at most $D/2$ satisfying
\[
 \operatorname{agr}_V(p,\beta\mapsto\beta^{2^{h-1}})\ge D.
\]
The maps are characterized by
\[
 \frac{\ell_V(X)}{g(X)}
   =\nu_V\bigl(p(X)^2+X\bigr),
 \qquad
 g(X)=\frac{\ell_V(X)}
 {\nu_V\bigl(p(X)^2+X\bigr)}.
\]
As in Proposition~\ref{prop:bijection}, the degree and agreement
inequalities are equalities.
head: environment
name: Additive-domain BCH--RS correspondence

title: Proof
body_md:
As in Proposition~\ref{prop:bijection}, the $n_0-D$
zeros of $g$ saturate the degree bound, so
$g\mid\ell_V$ and $b:=\ell_V/g$ has degree $D$,
with roots exactly where $g=1$. Differentiating
$bg=\ell_V$ at those roots gives $b'(\beta)=\nu_V$.
Because $\deg b'<D$, we have $b'\equiv\nu_V$,
and hence, in characteristic two, uniquely
\[
 b=\nu_V(p^2+X),\qquad \deg p=D/2.
\]
The $D$ roots give the required agreements with
$\beta^{2^{h-1}}$.

Conversely, such a polynomial $p$ yields
$b=\nu_V(p^2+X)$ of degree $D$ with $D$ distinct
roots in $V$ and derivative $\nu_V$. Thus
$b\mid\ell_V$; for $g=\ell_V/b$, the identity
$b'g+bg'=\nu_V$ shows that $g=1$ at those
roots and $g=0$ elsewhere on $V$.
This recovers the prescribed binary weight
and degree, and the constructions are inverse.
head: environment

label: def:anchor-family
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:anchor-family}
Fix an integer $c\ge0$. For each $h>c$, let
$V_h\le(\mathbb F_{2^h},+)$ be an additive subspace of
codimension $c$, and put $n_0:=|V_h|=2^{h-c}$.
A sequence $(\mathcal A_h)$ of nonempty sets
$\mathcal A_h\subseteq\mathbb F_{2^h}[X]$ is an
\emph{anchor family of codimension $c$}
(or \emph{density $\lambda=2^{-c}$}) if every
$p\in\mathcal A_h$ has degree $<n_0/4$ and
\[
 \min_{p\in\mathcal A_h}
 \frac{\operatorname{agr}_{V_h}(p,X^{2^{h-1}})}{n_0}
 \ge\tfrac12-o(1)\qquad(h\to\infty).
\]
head: environment
name: Anchor family

label: prop:classical-bch
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:classical-bch}
For all sufficiently large $h$, there is an even integer
$D_h^\star<2^{h-1}$ such that
\[
 \frac{D_h^\star}{2^h}=\frac12-o(1),\qquad
 A(2^h,D_h^\star)\ge2^{h^2/8-O(h)}.
\]
head: environment
name: BCH minimum-weight multiplicity

label: thm:anchor
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:anchor}
There is an anchor family $(\mathcal A_h)$ of codimension
$0$, with $V_h=\mathbb F_{2^h}$, such that for all sufficiently
large $h$,
\[
 |\mathcal A_h|\ge2^{h^2/8-O(h)}.
\]
Thus the full-field code $\operatorname{RS}_{\mathbb F_{2^h}}(2^{h-2})$
has a superpolynomial list at rate $1/4$
and limiting agreement $1/2$.
head: environment
name: Full-field anchor family

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:bijection} to the
$A(2^h,D_h^\star)$ weight-$D_h^\star$ BCH words supplied by
Proposition~\ref{prop:classical-bch}. This gives distinct messages
of degree $D_h^\star/2<2^{h-2}$, all agreeing with the received function
$\beta\mapsto\beta^{2^{h-1}}$ at exactly
$D_h^\star=(1/2-o(1))2^h$ points. Together they form
the claimed anchor family.
head: environment

label: prop:asymptotic-padding
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Padding an anchor family

title: Proof
body_md:
By the anchor-family definition, we may take
$\eta_h\to0$ such that each $p\in\mathcal A_h$
agrees with $\rho$ at no fewer than
$(1/2-\eta_h)n_0$ points of $V$.
Let $k=\lfloor Rn\rfloor$ and $b=k-n_0/4$.
For each padding set $T$ of size $b$,
use $z_T\rho$ as the received word
and $z_Tp$ as the padded messages.
Their distinctness is preserved by multiplication
by the same nonzero polynomial $z_T$.

\emph{Disjoint padding.}
If $b\le n-n_0$, choose $T\subseteq K\setminus V$.
All original anchor agreements survive and the
$b$ roots give additional agreements. Every padded
message therefore agrees at least
\[
 b+(1/2-\eta_h)n_0
\]
times. Dividing by $n$ gives the limiting fraction
\[
 \left(R-\frac{\lambda}{4}\right)
       +\frac{\lambda}{2}
 =R+\frac{\lambda}{4}.
\]
All $M_h$ messages are retained.

\emph{Overlapping padding.}
If $b>n-n_0$, use every point outside $V$ as a
padding root and choose the remaining roots
uniformly from $V$. Equivalently, the $n-b$
unpadded coordinates form a uniformly random
subset of $V$. A uniformly selected unpadded
coordinate is an agreement for a fixed anchor
$p$ with probability
$\operatorname{agr}_V(p,\rho)/n_0\ge1/2-\eta_h$.
Including the $b$ automatic agreements,
the expected number of agreements for each
padded message is at least
\[
 n\mu_h,\qquad
 \mu_h:=\frac bn+
          \left(1-\frac bn\right)
          \left(\frac12-\eta_h\right).
\]
Since $b/n\to R-\lambda/4$, we obtain
\[
 \mu_h\longrightarrow
 \frac{1+R}{2}-\frac{\lambda}{8}.
\]

We choose the \emph{same} random padding set for
all anchors. Averaging shows that some set $T$
gives an average of at least $n\mu_h$ agreements
across the $M_h$ messages. Put
$A=\lfloor n\mu_h\rfloor$. If $G$ messages have at least
$A$ agreements, the rest have at most $A-1$, so
\[
 M_hn\mu_h\le(M_h-G)(A-1)+Gn,
 \qquad
 G\ge\frac{M_h(n\mu_h-A+1)}{n-A+1}
 \ge\frac{M_h}{n}.
\]

At the switching rate $R=1-3\lambda/4$, we have
$b=n-n_0$ exactly, so the disjoint construction
uses every point outside $V$.
The rounding loss $1/n$ in the overlapping case
vanishes, proving the assertion for every fixed
$\alpha<\alpha_\lambda(R)$.
head: environment

label: cor:anchor-lifting
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:anchor-lifting}
For every fixed $1/4\le R<3/4$ and every fixed
$R<\alpha<3/8+R/2$, all sufficiently large $h$
admit a received word for the full-field RS code
over $\mathbb F_{2^h}$ of dimension $\lfloor R2^h\rfloor$
with at least $2^{h^2/8-O_{R,\alpha}(h)}$ codewords
at agreement fraction at least $\alpha$.
head: environment
name: Padding the full-field anchor family

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:anchor} gives anchor families
of codimension $0$ and size $2^{h^2/8-O(h)}$,
so $\lambda=1$. Padding is feasible at every
$R\ge1/4$, including equality. The overlapping
branch of~\eqref{eq:padding-agreement}
(or either branch at $R=1/4$) gives
\[
 \alpha_1(R)=\frac{1+R}{2}-\frac18
             =\frac38+\frac R2.
\]
This exceeds $R$ for $R<3/4$. The loss of
at most a factor $n=2^h$ preserves the
leading $h^2/8$ list-size exponent.
head: environment

label: def:W-invariant
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:W-invariant}
Let $W\le(K,+)$ be an additive subspace. A function
$f:K\to K$ is \emph{$W$-invariant} if
\[
 f(x+\omega)=f(x)\qquad
 \text{for every }x\in K\text{ and }\omega\in W.
\]
Equivalently, $f$ is constant on each coset of $W$.
This terminology also applies to $\mathbb F_2$-valued
functions on $K$.
head: environment
name: $W$-invariant function

label: def:quadratic-polar
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:quadratic-polar}
A map $\varphi:K\to\mathbb F_2$ is a \emph{quadratic form} if
$\varphi(0)=0$ and
\[
 B_\varphi(x,y):=\varphi(x+y)+\varphi(x)+\varphi(y)
\]
is bilinear over $\mathbb F_2$. The bilinear form $B_\varphi$ is the
\emph{polar form} of $\varphi$. Since $B_\varphi(x,x)=0$ for every $x$,
it is alternating.
head: environment
name: Quadratic form and polar form

label: def:radical-rank
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:radical-rank}
The \emph{polar radical} of $\varphi$ is
\[
 \operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)
 :=\{\omega\in K:B_\varphi(x,\omega)=0
       \text{ for every }x\in K\}.
\]
By bilinearity, $\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$ is a linear subspace of $K$.
The \emph{polar rank} is
\[
 \operatorname{rank}(B_\varphi)
 :=h-\dim_{\mathbb F_2}\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi).
\]
The polar form is \emph{nondegenerate} when $\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)=\{0\}$:
then no nonzero direction has zero polar interaction with every other
direction.
head: environment
name: Polar radical and polar rank

label: def:quadratic-rank
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:quadratic-rank}
The \emph{quadratic radical} of $\varphi$ is
\[
 \operatorname{rad}(\varphi)
 :=\{\omega\in\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi):\varphi(\omega)=0\}
 =\ker\bigl(\varphi|_{\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)}\bigr).
\]
The \emph{quadratic rank} is
\[
 \operatorname{rank}(\varphi)
 :=h-\dim_{\mathbb F_2}\operatorname{rad}(\varphi).
\]
head: environment
name: Quadratic radical and quadratic rank

label: ex:binary-quadratic
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:binary-quadratic}
On $U=\mathbb F_2^3$, consider
\[
 \varphi_0(x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_1x_2,
 \qquad
 \varphi_1(x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_1x_2+x_3.
\]
They have the same polar form
$B(x,y)=x_1y_2+x_2y_1$ and hence the same polar radical
\[
 \operatorname{rad}(B_{\varphi_0})
 =\operatorname{rad}(B_{\varphi_1})
 =\langle(0,0,1)\rangle.
\]
Their quadratic radicals differ:
\[
 \operatorname{rad}(\varphi_0)=\langle(0,0,1)\rangle,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{rad}(\varphi_1)=\{0\}.
\]
Thus both have polar rank $2$, but their quadratic ranks are
$2$ and $3$, respectively; their Hamming weights are $2$ and $4$.
Translation by $(0,0,1)$ fixes $\varphi_0$ but flips
$\varphi_1$. Adding the linear function $x_3$ to $\varphi_1$
recovers $\varphi_0$ and restores invariance.
head: environment
name: Polar and quadratic radicals

label: prop:even-polar-rank
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:even-polar-rank}
Every quadratic form $\varphi:K\to\mathbb F_2$ has even polar rank.
head: environment
name: Evenness of polar rank

title: Proof
body_md:
The alternating-form argument is given in
Appendix~\ref{app:quadratic-even-rank}.
head: environment

label: prop:quadratic-character-sum
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:quadratic-character-sum}
Let $\varphi:K\to\mathbb F_2$ be a quadratic form of quadratic rank $r$.
Then
\[
 \operatorname{wt}_K(\varphi)=
 \begin{cases}
  2^{h-1}\pm2^{h-a-1},&r=2a,\\
  2^{h-1},&r=2a+1.
 \end{cases}
\]
For even $r$, the sign depends on the quadratic form,
not just its quadratic rank.
head: environment
name: Quadratic rank and Hamming weight

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $S=\sum_{x\in K}(-1)^{\varphi(x)}$. Expanding $S^2$ and
using the bijection $(x,y)\mapsto(x,x+y)$ gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 S^2
 &=\sum_{x,y\in K}(-1)^{\varphi(x)+\varphi(y)}\\
 &=\sum_{x,z\in K}(-1)^{\varphi(x)+\varphi(x+z)}\\
 &=\sum_{z\in K}(-1)^{\varphi(z)}
     \sum_{x\in K}(-1)^{B_\varphi(x,z)}\\
 &=2^h\sum_{z\in \operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)}(-1)^{\varphi(z)}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The last equality evaluates the inner sum over $x$ in the third
line. For $z\notin \operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$, the map $x\mapsto B_\varphi(x,z)$
is a nonzero binary linear functional, so its character sum is
zero; for $z\in \operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$, that inner sum is $2^h$.

It remains to evaluate the sum over $z\in \operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$ in the last
line. As observed above,
$\varphi|_{\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)}$ is linear. If it is nonzero, this sum vanishes
and $S=0$. Otherwise it equals $|\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)|=2^{h-2a}$, since
the quadratic rank is then the polar rank $2a$. Hence
$S^2=2^{2h-2a}$. The identity
$\operatorname{wt}_K(\varphi)=(2^h-S)/2$ now gives the stated weights.
head: environment

label: lem:radical-shifts
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:radical-shifts}
Let $\varphi:K\to\mathbb F_2$ be a quadratic form of polar rank $2a$. Among all affine shifts $L+b$, with $L:K\to\mathbb F_2$
linear and $b\in\mathbb F_2$, exactly $2^{2a}$ choices make
$f=\varphi+L+b$ $\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$-invariant and have weight $D_{h,a}$.
For each selected linear
part $L$, the quadratic radical $\operatorname{rad}(\varphi+L)$ equals $\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$.
head: environment
name: Affine shifts adapted to a polar radical

title: Proof
body_md:
We first determine which linear parts $L$ make
$f=\varphi+L+b$ $\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$-invariant.
The translation identity shows that
\[
 L|_{\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)}=\varphi|_{\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)}
\]
is sufficient. It is also necessary: if $f$ is
$\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$-invariant, then for every $\omega\in \operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$,
\[
 0=f(\omega)+f(0)=\varphi(\omega)+L(\omega).
\]
As established above, $\varphi$ restricts to a linear functional on
its polar radical. This functional extends to $K$: extend a basis of $\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$ to a basis of $K$ and choose its
values arbitrarily on the added basis vectors. Any two extensions
differ by a linear functional that vanishes on $\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$, equivalently
by a linear functional on the quotient $K/\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$. Since this
quotient has dimension $2a$, there are exactly $2^{2a}$ extensions.

Fix one such extension $L$. The quadratic form $\varphi+L$ has the
same polar rank $2a$ and vanishes on $\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$, so its quadratic
rank is $2a$. Proposition~\ref{prop:quadratic-character-sum}
gives weight $2^{h-1}\pm2^{h-a-1}$. Adding the constant $b$
interchanges zeros and ones, so exactly one choice gives the
smaller weight $D_{h,a}$.

For each selected $L$, the quadratic form $\psi:=\varphi+L$
vanishes on its polar radical $\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$. Therefore
$\operatorname{rad}(\psi)=\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$ by the definition of the quadratic radical.
No other affine shifts satisfy both the invariance and weight requirements.
head: environment

label: lem:trace-degree
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:trace-degree}
Let $\varphi\in\mathcal F_{h,a}$ and let $f=\varphi+L+b$
for any affine shift $L+b$. If $c_f\in K[X]$ is the canonical
degree-$<2^h$ polynomial representing $f$ on $K$, then
\[
 \deg c_f\le 2^{h-1}+\delta.
\]
If in addition $\operatorname{wt}_K(f)=D_{h,a}$, then
\[
 \deg c_f=2^{h-1}+\delta.
\]
head: environment
name: Degree checkpoint for the trace-quadratic family

title: Proof
body_md:
First consider a quadratic trace term. Expanding gives
\[
 \operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb F_2}(uX^{2^i+1})
 =\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}
   u^{2^j}X^{2^{i+j}+2^j},
\]
where exponents are reduced as polynomial functions on $K$. Thus each
resulting exponent has two binary $1$-positions, obtained by cyclically
shifting the positions $0$ and $i$ modulo $h$; their circular
separations are $i$ and $h-i$. For the indices in
$\mathcal F_{h,a}$, both separations are at least $a$. Hence, if the
larger position is $h-1$, the other is at most $h-a-1$, and every such
exponent is at most
\[
 2^{h-1}+2^{h-a-1}=2^{h-1}+\delta.
\]
When $h=2m$, the remaining term
$\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_{2^m}/\mathbb F_2}(u_m X^{2^m+1})$ is the trace of
$u_m$ times the relative norm $X^{2^m+1}$ from $K$ to
$\mathbb F_{2^m}$. Its expansion has exponents
$2^{m+j}+2^j$ for $0\le j<m$, whose binary positions are
separated by $m$, so the same bound applies.
Finally, every $\mathbb F_2$-linear functional on $K$ has the form
$\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb F_2}(vX)$ for some $v\in K$.\footnote{This is the trace description of $\operatorname{RM}(1,h)$~\cite{DGM1970}; alternatively, the $2^h$ distinct maps $x\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}(vx)$ exhaust all $2^h$ binary linear functionals.}
Thus an affine shift $L+b$ has canonical degree at most
$2^{h-1}$ and does not increase the bound.

If $\operatorname{wt}_K(f)=D_{h,a}$, then $c_f$ has
$2^{h-1}+\delta$ zeros in $K$; the root bound forces equality
in the degree bound.
head: environment

label: prop:schmidt-form-count
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Schmidt's quadratic-form count

label: prop:enumeration
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:enumeration}
The $C_{h,a}$ forms in $\mathcal Q_{h,a}$ have polar rank
$2a$ and pairwise distinct polar forms. For each
$\varphi\in\mathcal Q_{h,a}$, exactly $2^{2a}$ affine
shifts belong to $\mathcal S_{h,a}$; they are
$\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$-invariant, satisfy $\operatorname{rad}(\varphi+L)=\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$,
and have canonical polynomial degree $2^h-D_{h,a}$.
The shifts associated with different $\varphi$ are distinct.
Consequently,
\[
 |\mathcal S_{h,a}|=2^{2a}C_{h,a}=:M_{h,a},
\]
and their canonical polynomials are distinct
weight-$D_{h,a}$ codewords of
$\operatorname{eBCH}(2^h,D_{h,a})$.
head: environment
name: Structured Schmidt subfamily

title: Proof
body_md:
We count the relevant Schmidt classes, identify their polar ranks,
and check that the affine shifts give distinct BCH words.

Proposition~\ref{prop:schmidt-form-count} supplies the
cardinality $C_{h,a}$.
The selected quadratic ranks are $2a+1$ (odd $h$) and $2a$
(even $h$, elliptic). By~\eqref{eq:quadratic-polar-rank} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:even-polar-rank}, both classes have
polar rank $2a$:
for odd $h$, the quadratic and polar ranks differ by one, whereas for even
$h$ they coincide. Thus their polar radicals have dimension
$h-2a$.

The selected forms have distinct polar forms: otherwise their
nonzero difference, still in the additive family $\mathcal F_{h,a}$,
would have zero polar form and hence be a nonzero linear function
of quadratic rank $1$, contradicting Schmidt's lower bound
$2a\ge2$ on quadratic rank stated above.

It remains to pass from the selected quadratic forms to BCH words.
Lemma~\ref{lem:radical-shifts} gives exactly $2^{2a}$ affine
shifts for each selected $\varphi$ that are
$\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$-invariant and have weight $D_{h,a}$. Since
$\mathcal Q_{h,a}\subseteq\mathcal F_{h,a}$, these shifts satisfy
both hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:trace-degree}, which gives
$\deg c_f=2^{h-1}+\delta=2^h-D_{h,a}$.
If two such functions from distinct selected $\varphi$ agreed,
their underlying quadratic forms would differ by a linear function,
contrary to the distinctness of the selected polar forms.
Their degree and weight place their canonical polynomials in
$\operatorname{eBCH}(2^h,D_{h,a})$ by~\eqref{eq:ebch-definition}.
Thus the disjoint contributions from the $C_{h,a}$
forms give $|\mathcal S_{h,a}|=2^{2a}C_{h,a}=M_{h,a}$.
head: environment

label: lem:subspace-descent
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Polynomial descent through a subspace quotient

title: Proof
body_md:
Polynomial descent and degree scaling here specialize
Berman--Shany--Tamo~\cite[Lemma~A.2]{BST}.
We give a direct proof that also establishes weight scaling
and the one-to-one correspondence.

\emph{(1) Polynomial descent.}
The subspace polynomial $\pi$ is $\mathbb F_2$-linear with kernel
$W$, and so induces an isomorphism $K/W\cong V$.
Both $f$ and $\pi$ are $W$-invariant, so each coset
$B=x+W$ determines a point
$(\pi(B),f(B))\in V\times\mathbb F_2$, where the two entries
denote their common values on $B$. The isomorphism
shows that the $n_0$ cosets have distinct
$\pi$-values, comprising all of $V$. Hence there is a unique
polynomial $f^{\downarrow}_W\in K[X]$ of degree $<n_0$ interpolating
these $n_0$ points. By construction,
$f(x)=f^{\downarrow}_W(\pi(x))$ for every $x\in K$.
As $\deg\pi=w$ and $wn_0=2^h$, the polynomial
$f^{\downarrow}_W\circ\pi$ has degree $<2^h$, as does $c_f$.
Since they agree throughout $K$, they coincide as
polynomials: $c_f=f^{\downarrow}_W\circ\pi$. The same interpolation
uniqueness shows that no other polynomial of degree $<n_0$
can satisfy this identity.

\emph{(2) Degree scaling.}
For $f^{\downarrow}_W\ne0$, polynomial composition gives
$\deg c_f=(\deg\pi)(\deg f^{\downarrow}_W)=w\deg f^{\downarrow}_W$,
including when $f^{\downarrow}_W$ is a nonzero constant.
If $f^{\downarrow}_W=0$, then $c_f=0$ by part~\textup{(1)},
so the identity holds
with the stated convention.

\emph{(3) Weight scaling.}
Each $\beta\in V$ has exactly $w$ preimages in $K$,
and $f$ takes the value $f^{\downarrow}_W(\beta)$ at all of them.
Counting ones and zeros gives the two scaling identities.

\emph{(4) One-to-one correspondence.}
Conversely, any polynomial $g$ of degree $<n_0$ that is
$\mathbb F_2$-valued on $V$ yields a $\mathbb F_2$-valued function
$g\circ\pi$ on $K$, which is $W$-invariant.
By uniqueness in part~\textup{(1)},
$(g\circ\pi)^{\downarrow}_W=g$. In the other direction,
part~\textup{(1)} gives $f=f^{\downarrow}_W\circ\pi$
as functions on $K$. These maps are inverse bijections,
and distinct canonical polynomials descend to distinct polynomials.
head: environment

label: prop:common-quotient-anchor
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:common-quotient-anchor}
There exists a $c$-dimensional additive subspace $W\le K$
such that
\[
 \bigl|\{f\in\mathcal S_{h,a}:
       f\text{ is }W\text{-invariant}\}\bigr|
 \ge\Gamma_{h,a,c}.
\]
With $V=\ell_W(K)$ of size $n_0$, these functions
yield at least $\Gamma_{h,a,c}$ distinct polynomials
$p_f\in K[X]$ of degree $D/2$, all agreeing with the same
received function
\[
 \rho(\beta)=\beta^{2^{h-1}}\qquad(\beta\in V)
\]
at exactly $D$ evaluation points, all of which belong to $V$.
head: environment
name: A common quotient RS anchor

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the incidence set
\[
 \mathcal I_{h,a,c}:=
 \bigl\{(f,W): f\in\mathcal S_{h,a},\
 W\le_{\mathbb F_2}K,\ \dim_{\mathbb F_2}W=c,\
 f\text{ is }W\text{-invariant}\bigr\}.
\]
For every $f=\varphi+L+b\in\mathcal S_{h,a}$,
its space of all invariant directions is
$\operatorname{rad}(\varphi+L)=\operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$, of dimension $h-2a$.
Hence $f$ is $W$-invariant precisely when
$W\subseteq \operatorname{rad}(B_\varphi)$, and
\[
 |\mathcal I_{h,a,c}|
 =|\mathcal S_{h,a}|\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{h-2a}{c}_{2}
 =M_{h,a}\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{h-2a}{c}_{2}.
\]
There are $\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{h}{c}_{2}$ possible $c$-dimensional
subspaces $W\le K$. Counting the pairs by their second
component therefore gives some $W$ for which at least
\[
 \frac{|\mathcal I_{h,a,c}|}{\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{h}{c}_{2}}
 =\Gamma_{h,a,c}
\]
members of $\mathcal S_{h,a}$ are $W$-invariant.

For this fixed $W$, Lemma~\ref{lem:subspace-descent}
gives distinct $\mathbb F_2$-valued polynomials
$f^{\downarrow}_W$ on the common domain $V$.
By degree and weight scaling, respectively,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \deg f^{\downarrow}_W
 &=\frac{\deg c_f}{2^c}
   =\frac{2^h-D_{h,a}}{2^c}
   =2^{h-c-1}+2^{h-a-c-1}=n_0-D,\\
 \operatorname{wt}_V(f^{\downarrow}_W)
 &=\frac{\operatorname{wt}_K(f)}{2^c}
   =\frac{D_{h,a}}{2^c}
   =2^{h-c-1}-2^{h-a-c-1}=D.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here $V=\ell_W(K)$ is an additive subspace, because
$\ell_W$ is $\mathbb F_2$-linear. Hence its subspace
polynomial $\ell_V$ has nonzero constant derivative,
as required in Proposition~\ref{prop:additive}.
Since $D$ is even and $2\le D<n_0$, that
correspondence yields distinct message polynomials
of degree
\[
 \deg p_f=\frac D2
 =2^{h-c-2}-2^{h-a-c-2},
\]
each with exactly $D$ agreements against
$\rho(\beta)=\beta^{2^{h-1}}$ on $V$.
Both the normalization and evaluation domain depend
only on $V$, so the received word is common to the family.
head: environment

label: cor:quotient-anchor-family
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:quotient-anchor-family}
For every fixed integer $c\ge0$, there is an anchor
family $(\mathcal A_h)$ of codimension $c$ satisfying
\[
 |\mathcal A_h|\ge2^{h^2/8-O_c(h)}
\]
for all sufficiently large $h$.
head: environment
name: Anchor families of prescribed codimension

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $m=\lfloor h/2\rfloor$. For fixed $c$ and feasible $a$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:counting-estimates} gives
\[
 \log_2\Gamma_{h,a,c}
 =2a(m-a)-2ac+O_c(h).
\]
The leading quadratic term is maximized near $a=m/2$,
while selecting a common $c$-dimensional subspace costs
only $O_c(h)$ bits. We therefore take $a=\lceil m/2\rceil$.
For fixed $c$ and large $h$, the constraints
$c\le h-2a$ and $h-a-c-1\ge1$ hold, so
Proposition~\ref{prop:common-quotient-anchor} applies.
Let $V_h=\ell_W(K)$ be the resulting common domain,
of codimension $c$. Its messages have degree
$D/2<|V_h|/4$ and agree with the received function at
\[
 D=\frac{|V_h|}{2}-2^{h-a-c-1}
    =\bigl(\tfrac12-o(1)\bigr)|V_h|
\]
coordinates. These polynomials form an anchor
family of codimension $c$. Moreover, this choice gives
\[
 \log_2\Gamma_{h,a,c}=h^2/8-O_c(h).
\]
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Classical BCH down-conversion, used in Kasami--Lin's
minimum-distance work and revisited by Berman--Shany--Tamo,
passes from suitable BCH codewords to lower-weight words
of smaller designed distance~\cite{KasamiLin,BST}.
The identity $c_f=f^{\downarrow}_W\circ\ell_W$ expresses
the corresponding descent in the polynomial model:
$W$-invariance permits passage to a smaller additive
evaluation domain, scaling both weight and degree by
$|W|$. The additional ingredient here is a common $W$
for superpolynomially many words, so their distinctness
and multiplicity survive the descent.
head: environment
name: Relation to classical down-conversion

label: prop:optimal-agreement-envelope
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:optimal-agreement-envelope}
For every $0<R<1$, the density $\lambda_*(R)$ defined above
maximizes $\alpha_\lambda(R)$ over all feasible dyadic choices
$\lambda=2^{-c}\le4R$. In particular,
\[
 \alpha_*(R)
 =\alpha_{\lambda_*(R)}(R)
 =\max_{c\ge0:\,2^{-c}\le4R}\alpha_{2^{-c}}(R).
\]
head: environment
name: Optimality of the dyadic agreement envelope

label: thm:allrate
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:allrate}
Fix $0<R<1$ and let $\alpha_*(R)$ be defined by
\eqref{eq:optimized-agreement-envelope}. For every fixed
$R<\alpha<\alpha_*(R)$, there exists $h_0=h_0(R,\alpha)$
such that all $h\ge h_0$ admit a received word for the
full-field RS code over $\mathbb F_{2^h}$ of dimension
$\lfloor R2^h\rfloor$ with at least
\[
 2^{h^2/8-O_R(h)}
\]
codewords at agreement fraction at least $\alpha$.
head: environment
name: All-rate full-field RS lower bound

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $R$ and $\alpha$ as in the statement, and choose the
optimal dyadic density $\lambda=\lambda_*(R)=2^{-c}\le4R$.
Corollary~\ref{cor:quotient-anchor-family} supplies
$h_1=h_1(R)$ such that every $h\ge h_1$ admits an anchor
family on a common additive domain of density $\lambda$
and size at least $2^{h^2/8-O_c(h)}$.
Since $\alpha<\alpha_\lambda(R)=\alpha_*(R)$,
Proposition~\ref{prop:asymptotic-padding} supplies
$h_2=h_2(R,\alpha)$ such that, for every $h\ge h_2$,
padding retains at least a $2^{-h}$ fraction of this family
at agreement fraction at least $\alpha$.
Taking $h_0=\max\{h_1,h_2\}$ and using that $c$ depends
only on $R$ gives $2^{h^2/8-O_R(h)}$ messages
for every $h\ge h_0$, as claimed.
head: environment

label: cor:densepuncture
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:densepuncture}
Fix $0<r<1$, put $G_r:=\alpha_*(r)-r>0$, and choose
$0<\theta<\min\{G_r,1-r\}$. For every fixed
$0<\xi<(G_r-\theta)/(1-\theta)$
and all sufficiently large $h$, if at most $\theta2^h$
coordinates are deleted from the full-field code
$\operatorname{RS}_{\mathbb F_{2^h}}(\lfloor r2^h\rfloor)$, the punctured
code has at least $2^{h^2/8-O_r(h)}$ distinct codewords
agreeing with one common received word on a fraction
of coordinates exceeding the punctured code's rate by at least
\[
 \frac{G_r-\theta}{1-\theta}-\xi,
\]
uniformly over the deleted set.
head: environment
name: Robustness under arbitrary dense puncturing

title: Remark
body_md:
The primitive RS family is a special case of
Corollary~\ref{cor:densepuncture}. For any target rate
$0<R<1$, choose a source rate $r<R$ sufficiently close to
$R$ that $\alpha_*(r)>R$, and then choose $\theta,\xi>0$
small enough that the surviving agreement exceeds $R$.
Deleting the coordinate $0$ and using
$\lfloor r2^h\rfloor\le\lfloor R(2^h-1)\rfloor$
for large $h$ gives a superpolynomial list in the
primitive code at rate $R$.

The same corollary transfers to arbitrary dense
\emph{shortenings}. Write $K=\mathbb F_{2^h}$ and
$k=\lfloor r2^h\rfloor$. For $U\subseteq K$ with
$t=|U|\le\theta|K|$, first apply the corollary to
$\operatorname{RS}_K(k)$ punctured on $U$. Since $k+t\le |K|$
for large $h$, that punctured code is monomially
equivalent to the shortening of $\operatorname{RS}_K(k+t)$ on $U$:
after deleting $U$, the latter consists of evaluations
of $z_U p$ with $\deg p<k$.
Dividing the surviving coordinates by the nonzero
values of $z_U$ identifies this code with
$\operatorname{RS}_{K\setminus U}(k)$, preserving Hamming
agreements and list sizes. Hence the corollary's
puncturing bound transfers to these shortened
codes.
head: environment
name: Primitive and shortened RS codes

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $B$ be an alternating bilinear form on a binary vector space.
If $B=0$, its rank is zero. Otherwise choose $x,y$ with $B(x,y)=1$
and put $W=\langle x,y\rangle$. The restriction $B|_W$ is
nondegenerate: if $a x+b y$ is orthogonal to both $x$ and $y$, then
$B(ax+by,x)=b$ and $B(ax+by,y)=a$, so $a=b=0$.
For any vector $v$, the vector
\[
 v+B(v,y)x+B(v,x)y
\]
is orthogonal to $W$. Hence the ambient space decomposes as
$W\oplus W^\perp$, and
\[
 \operatorname{rank} B
 =2+\operatorname{rank}(B|_{W^\perp}).
\]
Iterating proves that the rank is even.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the additive family $\mathcal F_{h,a}$ and a specified
class $\mathcal C$ of quadratic forms, Schmidt's normalized
inner-distribution coefficient is
\[
 \frac{1}{|\mathcal F_{h,a}|}
 \left|\{(\varphi,\varphi')\in\mathcal F_{h,a}^2:
                 \varphi-\varphi'\in\mathcal C\}\right|.
\]
Every fixed difference occurs exactly $|\mathcal F_{h,a}|$
times, so the coefficient counts individual forms of
$\mathcal F_{h,a}$ in $\mathcal C$.
For odd $h=2m+1$, set $q=2$, $d=2a+1$ in Schmidt's
Theorem~5.4, and $s=a+1$ in Theorem~4.7.
For even $h=2m$, set $q=2$ and Schmidt's parameter
$\delta_{\mathrm{Sch}}=a$ in Theorem~5.6, and take $s=a$,
$\tau=-1$ (the elliptic class) in Theorem~4.9.
The Gaussian coefficients use base $q^2=4$, giving
the two cases of~\eqref{eq:Cha}.
head: environment

label: lem:counting-estimates
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:counting-estimates}
Fix an integer $c\ge0$ and put $m=\lfloor h/2\rfloor$.
Uniformly for $1\le a\le m$ satisfying
$c\le h-2a$ and $h-a-c-1\ge1$,
\[
 \log_2\Gamma_{h,a,c}
 =2a(m-a)-2ac+O_c(h).
\]
head: environment
name: Common-quotient multiplicity estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
We first estimate the Gaussian coefficients used below.
For any prime power $r$ and integers $m\ge0$, $0\le a\le m$,
\[
 \genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{m}{a}_{r}
 =r^{a(m-a)}
 \prod_{j=0}^{a-1}
 \frac{1-r^{-(m-j)}}{1-r^{-(a-j)}}.
\]
Each ratio is at least one since $m-j\ge a-j$,
while the product is at most
\[
 C_r:=\prod_{t=1}^{\infty}(1-r^{-t})^{-1}<\infty.
\]
The infinite product converges because
$\sum_{t\ge1}r^{-t}<\infty$. Consequently,
\[
 \log_r\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{m}{a}_{r}=a(m-a)+O_r(1),
\]
uniformly in $m$ and $a$.

Next, Proposition~\ref{prop:schmidt-form-count} and the
definition of $M_{h,a}$ give
\[
 M_{h,a}=2^{2a}(2^{t_h}-1)\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{m}{a}_{4},
 \qquad
 t_h=\begin{cases}
 h,&h=2m+1,\\
 a,&h=2m.
 \end{cases}
\]
Using the Gaussian estimate with $r=4$ and
$2^{t_h-1}\le 2^{t_h}-1\le 2^{t_h}$ yields
\[
 \log_2 M_{h,a}
 =2a(m-a)+2a+t_h+O(1)
 =2a(m-a)+O(h).
\]

Finally, the definition of $\Gamma_{h,a,c}$ gives
\[
 \frac{\Gamma_{h,a,c}}{M_{h,a}}
 =\frac{\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{h-2a}{c}_{2}}{\genfrac{[}{]}{0pt}{}{h}{c}_{2}}
 =2^{-2ac}P_{h,a,c},
 \qquad
 P_{h,a,c}:=\prod_{j=0}^{c-1}
 \frac{1-2^{-(h-2a-j)}}{1-2^{-(h-j)}}.
\]
For $c\le h-2a$, every factor of $P_{h,a,c}$
is at most one and at least $1-2^{-(c-j)}$.
Consequently,
\[
 0<\prod_{t=1}^{c}(1-2^{-t})
 \le P_{h,a,c}\le1.
\]
The empty product is one for $c=0$. Since $c$
is fixed, taking logarithms gives
\[
 \log_2\frac{\Gamma_{h,a,c}}{M_{h,a}}
 =-2ac+O_c(1).
\]
Combining the shifted-family and quotient estimates
proves the lemma.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $m=\lfloor h/2\rfloor$. For every $1\le a\le m$, Proposition~\ref{prop:enumeration}
gives $A(2^h,D_{h,a})\ge M_{h,a}$.
Taking $c=0$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:counting-estimates},
so that $\Gamma_{h,a,0}=M_{h,a}$, gives
\[
 \log_2 M_{h,a}=2a(m-a)+O(h).
\]
Choose $a=\lceil m/2\rceil$, which maximizes
the quadratic term up to rounding, and put
$D_h^\star:=D_{h,a}$. Then
\[
 \log_2 M_{h,a}=\frac{h^2}{8}+O(h),
 \qquad
 \frac{D_h^\star}{2^h}=\frac12-2^{-a-1}=\frac12-o(1).
\]
For sufficiently large $h$,
$D_h^\star=2^{h-1}-2^{h-a-1}$ is even
and strictly smaller than $2^{h-1}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $g=1-R$ and $G_\lambda(R)=\alpha_\lambda(R)-R$.
Section~\ref{sec:rate-lifting} gives
\[
 G_\lambda(R)=
 \begin{cases}
 \lambda/4,&\lambda\le4g/3,\\
 g/2-\lambda/8,&\lambda\ge4g/3.
 \end{cases}
\]
Thus the gain increases with $\lambda$ in the disjoint
regime and decreases in the overlapping regime.

First suppose $0<R<1/4$. Then $4R<4g/3$,
so every feasible density $\lambda\le4R$ is
disjoint. Write $2^{-j}\le R<2^{-j+1}$ with
$j\ge3$. The largest feasible dyadic density is
$\lambda_*=2^{-j+2}$, and its agreement is
\[
 \alpha_*(R)=R+\lambda_*/4=R+2^{-j}.
\]

Now suppose $R\ge1/4$ and write
$2^{-j}\le g<2^{-j+1}$ with $j\ge1$.
All dyadic densities at most one are feasible.
Set $d=2^{-j+1}$, so
\[
 d/2\le g<d,\qquad d\le1.
\]
Every other dyadic density is at most $d/2$
or at least $2d$. If $\lambda\le d/2$,
then $\lambda\le g<4g/3$, so it is disjoint
and $G_\lambda(R)\le d/8$.
If $d$ is disjoint, $G_d(R)=d/4$; if $d$
is overlapping, then
\[
 G_d(R)=g/2-d/8\ge d/8.
\]
Thus no smaller density improves on $d$
(equality is possible when $g=d/2$).

If $\lambda\ge2d$, then $\lambda>4g/3$,
so it is overlapping, with
\[
 G_\lambda(R)=g/2-\lambda/8
 \le g/2-d/4.
\]
For overlapping $d$ this is strictly smaller
than $G_d(R)=g/2-d/8$.
For disjoint $d$, it is smaller than
$d/4=G_d(R)$, since $g<d$.
Hence $d$ is also optimal among all feasible
dyadic densities.

For this fixed optimal density, the switch between
disjoint and overlapping padding occurs at
\[
 g=3d/4=3\cdot2^{-j-1},
 \qquad R=1-3\cdot2^{-j-1}.
\]
For $j\ge2$, this lies strictly inside the dyadic
interval $1-2^{-j+1}<R\le1-2^{-j}$.
For $j=1$, it occurs at the endpoint $R=1/4$.
Consequently the two affine pieces within a high-rate
dyadic interval come from the padding-regime transition;
changes of the optimal density at dyadic endpoints are a
different phenomenon. Substituting $d=2^{-j+1}$
into the two padding formulas yields
\eqref{eq:optimized-agreement-envelope}.
At $g=d/2$ an adjacent dyadic density ties,
which justifies the half-open dyadic intervals.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $G_r=\alpha_*(r)-r$, as in the corollary.
Use Theorem~\ref{thm:allrate} at the fixed source agreement
$r+G_r-\eta$, where $0<\eta<G_r-\theta$.
Delete $t\le\theta2^h$ coordinates from the full-field code.
Every message loses at most $t$ agreements, while its degree
remains below $k=\lfloor r2^h\rfloor$ and the punctured
length $2^h-t$ eventually exceeds $k$ because
$\theta<1-r$. Thus distinctness survives, and the new
agreement-minus-rate gap is at least
\[
 \frac{(r+G_r-\eta)2^h-t-k}{2^h-t}
 \ge\frac{G_r-\eta-\theta}{1-\theta}-o(1).
\]
Choose $\eta<\min\{G_r-\theta,(1-\theta)\xi/2\}$
and then take $h$ sufficiently large.
